Noise
noiz
n. (a loud or confused sound; clamour; rendering Hebrew qol, hamon, and shaon)
From Old French noise, quarrel or uproar, probably from the Latin nausea by way of the din of a seasick ship's company — a disputed derivation, but the sense of confused and unwelcome sound is ancient in the word.

Biblical Definition

Noise is sound without discernible sense, and Scripture handles it with a striking evenhandedness. It can be misread: coming down from the mount, “when Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said unto Moses, There is a noise of war in the camp” (Exodus 32:17). It was not war; it was idolatry, which from a distance sounds much the same. It can be genuinely indistinguishable: at the laying of the second temple's foundation, “the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people” (Ezra 3:13) — the young rejoicing and the old men who remembered the first house wept, and the two made one sound. Few verses describe the mingled state of God's people in this world so exactly. It is also what God silences: he “stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people” (Psalm 65:7), the three set side by side because the roaring of the nations is no harder for him than the roaring of the surf. Most soberly, worship itself can become noise in God's ears when the life behind it is corrupt: “Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols” (Amos 5:23). What Israel called music, God called racket.

Webster 1828 Definition

Loud or confused sound. Scripture shows it misread, shows joy and grief making one indistinguishable noise, shows God stilling it — and warns that unfaithful worship reaches him only as noise.

expand to see more

NOISE, n. noiz. [Fr. noise, a quarrel.] Sound of any kind, or proceeding from any cause; but chiefly, loud, confused, or stunning sound.

2. Outcry; clamor; loud complaint or importunity.

3. Frequent talk; much public conversation; as, to make a noise in the world.

4. NOISE, v.i. To sound loud; to make an outcry.

5. NOISE, v.t. To spread by rumor or report; as, it was noised abroad that he was come.

Key Scripture

Exodus 32:17 — "And when Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said unto Moses, There is a noise of war in the camp."

Ezra 3:13 — "So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people: for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard afar off."

Psalm 65:7 — "Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people."

Amos 5:23 — "Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols."

Modern Corruption

Amos 5:23 is the standing rebuke to worship offered by an unjust people, yet it is seldom preached — while a general appetite for loudness makes it harder than ever to distinguish sound from noise.

expand to see more

Amos is speaking to a people whose services were full and whose scales were false. Into that setting God says he hates their feast days, will not smell in their solemn assemblies, and wants the noise of their songs taken away — and then names what he does want: judgment running down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream (Amos 5:24). The passage is not a criticism of music; it is a verdict on worship detached from obedience. It should be preached wherever a congregation is more careful about its sound than about its dealings. God is not obliged to receive as praise what a corrupt life offers him, and he says so in the plainest terms available.

The principle to recover is Ezra 3:13 — that in this world the joy and the grief of God's people are often one sound, and that God hears both accurately even when the bystanders cannot tell them apart. The men who wept had seen the first house; the men who shouted had only ever heard of it. Both responses were right. A congregation containing the elderly who remember better days and the young who are glad of what they have is not divided; it is normal, and the noise it makes together is heard in heaven as two distinct things.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qol is sound or voice generally; hamon is a multitude and the roar it makes; shaon is a crash or uproar, used of the seas and of war.

expand to see more

Hebrew qol (H6963) — voice, sound, noise; the general word, judged by context.

Hebrew hamon (H1995) — a multitude, and the tumult it makes; the noise of many peoples.

Hebrew shaon (H7588) — a crash, roar, uproar; the noise of the seas in Psalm 65:7.

Hebrew teruah (H8643) — a shout, alarm, or blast; the shout of joy in Ezra 3.

Greek thorubos (G2351) — an uproar, tumult, disorderly noise of a crowd.

Usage

"Of noise misread from a distance: there is a noise of war in the camp (Exodus 32:17)."

"Of joy and grief indistinguishable: could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping (Ezra 3:13)."

"Of worship rejected as mere noise: take thou away from me the noise of thy songs (Amos 5:23)."
